catalogs.context:
The tile speaks to where the person is with Ari. A stranger (anonymous,
or a host with no user facade at all) is asked in; someone logged in is
greeted as a regular. The lead asks for the account and goes quiet once
there is one. Location is not its ask any more: a wall without a fix
stands on Zürich HB and the grid's placement notice, right under this
tile, asks for the real one (grid/placement-notice-strings.ts), so the two
never say the same thing. Bracketed words are the underlined links
(preview.ts renderLead).

Vocabulary follows the account flow the tap opens: a stranger is on an
anonymous session with no account yet, so the ask is to SIGN UP (iOS
settings: "Create your account" / "Erstelle dein Konto"), never to sign
in — ari-landing's pair is "Log in" + "Sign up", "Anmelden" +
"registrieren"/"Konto erstellen". Sign-in words are for people who
already have an account (wording decision 2026-09-04).

keys.de: [Erstelle dein Konto], damit Ari deins wird.

catalogs.context:
What's On — everything the widget prints, in the reader's language.

Organised by surface, not alphabetically: a translator works through one
screen at a time, and a key's neighbours should be the words next to it on
that screen.

Two rules this file exists to keep:

1. **A label is never an id.** `humanizeTag()` feeds the chip display
label AND the search token index; the category keys feed the facet
filter. Translating those in place would break query parsing and
filtering. So display labels live here, keyed BY the English id, and
the id itself is never touched — the same split PR #1371 made for
`widget-rating`, and why a German user picking 'Info fehlt' still
persists `Missing info`.
2. **Numbers, dates and distances belong to `Intl`,** not to a template
in here. German writes '1,2 km' and 'Mi., 26. Aug.'. This file holds
the words around the number; `formatters(formatLocale)` holds the
number.

Query vocabulary — the German words a person TYPES — lives next door in
`search-vocabulary.ts`. Translating what we print and understanding what
they write are different jobs, and only one of them is copy.
